title: 15-minute chair workout for ages 50 and above
intro: No gym needed, no expensive sportswear. A sturdy chair is enough. This 15-minute routine suits you if you are just starting, have knee pain, or worry about your balance. You can do it at home, even at the office during a break.

sections.p: Choose a sturdy chair without wheels, and without armrests if possible. Place the chair against a wall so it won't slip. Wear comfortable clothes and shoes, or go barefoot on a non-slippery floor. Have a glass of water ready. If you check your own blood sugar and take medicine that can lower sugar, keep a little sweet food nearby, for example a few dates or sweets.

Sit up straight. March your feet gently on the spot, left and right, for 1 minute while swinging your arms. Then roll your shoulders backward 10 times and forward 10 times. Finally, slowly turn your head to the left and right, 5 times each side. Breathe normally, don't hold your breath.

Do each move for about 1 minute, rest 30 seconds, then repeat all of them once more. 1) Sit-to-stand: stand up from the chair, sit back down slowly. You can use your hands. 2) Seated knee lifts: lift the left knee, lower, lift the right knee, like marching while seated. 3) Leg straightening: straighten one leg, hold 2 seconds, lower, switch legs. 4) Wall push-up: stand a little away from the wall, put your palms on the wall at shoulder level, bend your elbows and push back. 5) Heel raises: stand behind the chair, hold on, rise onto your toes and lower slowly.

Sit back down. Stretch the back of your thigh by straightening one leg and leaning slightly forward, hold 20 seconds each leg. Hug yourself to stretch the back of your shoulders, hold 20 seconds. Take 5 deep breaths. Drink water.

sections.h: How often and when to add more
sections.p: Start with 3 days a week, for example Monday, Wednesday and Friday. If it feels easy after 2 to 3 weeks, you can add one more round or do it 4 to 5 days a week. A good guide: you can still talk while exercising, but feel a little tired. The next day your body may feel a bit achy, that is normal.

action: Find a sturdy chair at home today and place it against a wall.
Do this 15-minute routine 3 times this week, for example after Subuh prayers or before dinner.
If you're busy, doing half the routine (7 minutes) is already good.
Count how many sit-to-stands you can do in 30 seconds, record it, and test again after a month.
doctor: See a doctor first if you have ever had chest pain, a heart attack or a stroke; if your blood pressure is not yet controlled or you often feel dizzy when standing; if you have fallen in the last 6 months; or if you were recently discharged from hospital or had surgery. Stop immediately and get help if you feel chest pain, severe breathlessness, spinning dizziness or unusual heart pounding during exercise. If you take medicine for high blood pressure or diabetes, do not change your medicine on your own. Tell your doctor you have started exercising so they can monitor you.

faq.a: Yes. For people who are just starting or have joint problems, chair exercises can help strengthen leg muscles, improve balance and make the body more active. What matters is doing them consistently, not once in a while.

faq.q: Can I do this at the office?
faq.a: Yes. Seated knee lifts, leg straightening and shoulder rolls can be done at your desk. You can also do a few sit-to-stands every hour. It also cuts down on sitting for too long.

faq.q: When is the best time to do it?
faq.a: The best time is the time you can stick to every week. Many like mornings, some prefer evenings. If you have diabetes, light movement about 15 to 30 minutes after eating can help blood sugar, but avoid exercising when your stomach is too full.
